1:
The occasion is settled quickly, the temper slowly. Clarke refers the psalm to the persecution by Saul, but collects the alternatives: the Syriac makes it composed when the Idumeans attacked David, the Arabic a prophecy of the incarnation, and some hold a later section applies more literally to Christ than to anyone else. Delitzsch pairs it with the psalm before as the only two naming the Angel of the Lord, and calls it the lyrical expansion of what David says to Saul's face in Samuel. He rejects the conjecture that Jeremiah wrote it, the opening verses suiting a persecuted king and not a prophet, and takes the points of contact for that prophet's recollections of an earlier author. Calvin describes the court: the nobles, in the subservient spirit that always prevails at the courts of kings, conspired against an innocent man and drew the common people into their hatred. But David knew most were carried by ignorance, and accounts as enemies only those who from deliberate malice worked to please Saul.

What the psalm asks is read in two registers at once. Ellicott insists the first verb be rendered strive rather than plead, since the construction requires it and the parallelism suggests recourse to arms rather than law; and he notices that the second verb is literally devour, comparing Shakespeare on the wars eating us up. Clarke keeps the law-court, translating contend and noting the word is often forensic. Spurgeon takes both at once: if they urge their suit in the law-court, meet them there and beat them at their own weapons; if they try force as well, oppose thy strength to theirs. The accuser of the brethren shall be met by the Advocate of the saints, and what is asked as a boon may be taken as a promise. Gill reads it of Christ committing himself to him that judgeth righteously, and of his people leaving their cause with their advocate, who pleads it against wicked men, against the accuser, and against their own hearts.

Calvin draws the practical use. David pleads for redress of both grievances: by appealing for aid in his cause he shows he has to do with maligning men, by urging God to take up arms that he was grievously oppressed. If David did not escape the malice of wicked men, it should not seem strange that they blame and bite at us; and though calumniators tear us to pieces by false charges, there is incomparable consolation in this, that God himself interposes against false accusations.

The armed figure of the second verse draws most of the comment. Ellicott corrects the order to buckler and shield, the first small and the second covering the whole body, and notices what the others pass over: in the intensity of his purpose the poet overlooks the anomaly of arming a warrior with two shields at once — a lapse excused by the bold imagination that pictures God as a warrior, an image common in Hebrew poetry but nowhere so vivid except in Isaiah. Spurgeon reads it as vivid metaphor, the Lord coming forth armed and interposing between his servant and his enemies, the two weapons perhaps standing for the greater and lesser protections of providence. Gill guards the figure against literalism — not that the Lord needs these to defend himself, but that he would be these to David, as he is to all his people. Clarke guards it more bluntly: it is by the shield and buckler of others, not any of his own, that God overthrows the enemies of his people, and the verse is spoken merely after the manner of men. Augustine reads the arms allegorically, the shield being the good-will with which God compasses his own; Henry sums the situation — if a fellow-subject had wronged him David might have appealed to his prince, but when the prince wronged him he appealed to God.
3:
The weapons of the third verse invite conjecture. Ellicott takes the spear as drawn from a sheath that guarded its point, and proposes that the next word, rendered stop the way by every version, is not a verb at all but the name of a Persian weapon mentioned by Herodotus and Xenophon, generally taken for a battle-axe — a rendering that makes an excellent parallelism and suits the word translated against, which really means to meet. Clarke and Wesley take the next clause as an assurance sought: say to my soul that thou art my salvation, the Spirit assuring it and providence effecting it.

The imprecations that follow are the real difficulty, and two readers defend them. Gill treats them as prophecies of what would be, not to be imitated by private persons, nor contrary to the rules requiring men to love their enemies. He shows how they were fulfilled, Saul being filled with shame when David held up the skirt he had cut off, proving that a life in his hands had been spared. Clarke defends them on another ground, that they are directed not against the souls of the men but against their schemes for destroying an innocent life: if a man aims a mortal blow, and the one attacked can prevent his own death and save his enemy from murder by breaking his arm, it is his duty to prevent that double evil.

The instruments of the pursuit are disputed. Clarke will not decide whether the angel means a spirit, good or bad, or anything God uses. Ellicott has no such hesitation: the angel of the Lord here personifies the hurricane, which drives all obstacles before it and overwhelms whole armies in dangerous places. On the dark and slippery way he rejects a suggested allusion to the Red Sea, preferring a mountain pass in a storm, and quotes the observation that the tracks in the limestone hills of Palestine are often worn as smooth as marble; Clarke reads the whole series as military language — ambushes, snares, forced marches, stratagems.

Two verses are thought disordered. Clarke says the word for pit belongs to the second member of the seventh verse: without cause they have hidden their net for me, without cause digged a pit for my life. Ellicott argues the same emendation, since as the text stands it can only mean a pit with a net in it. Delitzsch agrees, and adds that two verbs in the fifth and sixth verses have likewise been exchanged. At the eighth verse Ellicott finds the versions pointing to confusion in the text, makes the pronouns plural, and notes that the word rendered destruction means primarily a storm. Gill takes the storm literally, of the sudden south wind of the East, and reports that some Jewish commentators refer the singular to Saul and some Christian interpreters to Judas.

The turn to joy is marked by all. Delitzsch observes that the bones, which elsewhere share only the anguish of the soul, here share its joy, so that gladness throbs through every member. Gill says soul and bones together design the whole man. Ellicott renders it as we would say all the fibres of my body, and corrects the twice-repeated poor to sufferer. Clarke draws a maxim: God is peculiarly mindful of the poor, since where secular advantages are withheld there is more need of spiritual help. On the false witnesses Henry reconstructs the proceeding: Saul probably had David attainted with the formalities of a prosecution, producing witnesses who swore to treasonable words. See, he says, how much the honours, estates and lives of the best men lie at the mercy of the worst, against whose false oaths innocence is no defence. Spurgeon adds that David was not only innocent but ignorant of the fault alleged, and it is well when our hands are so clean no trace of dirt is on them.
12:
The ingratitude is stated first: for killing Goliath and saving king and country, Gill says, David was envied and hunted. Clarke corrects the rendering, the word translated soul here meaning life; Ellicott gives the clause literally as desolation to my soul.

What David did for them when they were sick occupies the readers longest. Clarke thinks it may refer to Absalom, and takes the returning prayer to mean that though the profligate did not profit by it God did not let him pray in vain: the prayers were like alms, returned tenfold into the bosom — where the Asiatics carry their purses and whatever is given them. Wesley says only that the fastings did them no good. Ellicott surveys the explanations and rejects three. Fruitless prayer must go, since the context implies something done for these one-time friends; so must the notion that the answer came back to the psalmist instead of to those prayed for; and so must silent prayer, since all the visible signs of mourning are named. What remains is the literal sense, that the prayer turned upon his bosom, referring to the posture of the next verse — a reading he calls prosaic.

The mourning is filled out from custom. Ellicott renders the next line I went squalid, and bowed down, alluding to the neglected beard and the dust and ashes of Eastern mourning. Clarke fastens on two words: as a mourning mother — how expressive is this word. Gill takes the friend or brother for Saul or Doeg, and compares Christ calling Judas friend, who not only ate at his table but carried the bag.

Two words in the next verses defeat everybody. Clarke makes the abjects smiters, hired assassins. Ellicott reports that the Hebrew occurs only here and has a perplexing form: the versions all give it an active sense — whips, smiters, the wicked who smite me with their words — while the passive rendering that yields our abjects comes from a mediaeval rabbi.

The hypocritical mockers in feasts Ellicott calls full of difficulty. The versions take the word rendered feasts as a cognate of one meaning barbarisms, and the word rendered hypocritical more properly means profane; with those senses the line reads in the manner of profane barbaric barbarisms, referring to the attacks of foreigners. The rendering feasts comes from treating the word as the one used for a cake, so the phrase means cake-mockers, parasites who hang about the tables of the rich and get their dinner for their buffooneries. Gill arrives independently at the same picture: they mocked David as wanting a piece of bread, or mocked him for the sake of a meal. Wesley states it plainly: they made themselves buffoons to deride David, that they might gain admittance to the tables of great men. Clarke leaves the philology alone and reads the verses as prophetic of Christ: they blindfolded and buffeted him so he could not discern who struck him, and the mocking in feasts may point to Herod's purple robe and reed.

Henry gathers the indictment. They were unrighteous, hating him without a cause and for what should rather have earned love — words quoted afterwards of Christ. They were rude, wanting the manners to give him the time of day, like Joseph's brethren who could not speak peaceably to him. They were proud, bawling after him when he had to quit the court, and barbarous, trampling him when he was down, as the Roman crowd execrated the fallen. And they devised deceitful matters against the quiet in the land — for it is the character of the godly to be quiet, living in dutiful subjection and endeavouring to live peaceably with all men, however they be misrepresented as enemies to Caesar; yet all the arts of malice are used to make them odious, their words misconstrued, and laws made to ensnare them.
18:
The vow of thanksgiving is read as an exile's hope. Clarke takes it as the hope of attending the tabernacle again and publicly expressing gratitude; Wesley reduces it to a clause, when I shall be restored to the liberty of the public assemblies. Gill fills out the thanks — acknowledging God the author of the mercy and himself unworthy. Delitzsch marks the formal change: the third part renews the description of the enemies' godlessness, but the psalmist's soul has grown more tranquil, and the language moves with its old calmness.

The winking eye is identified from custom. Ellicott calls it a gesture of agreement among confederates. Delitzsch works the verb: it means both to nip and to compress, and is used of the lips as well as the eyes, always as an insidiously malicious gesture. Spurgeon reads it as the low-bred sign of congratulation at a victim's ruin, and adds a rule: to cause hatred is the mark of the wicked, to suffer it causelessly the lot of the righteous. Gill makes a grammatical point: wrongfully belongs not to rejoice but to enemies, so the complaint is of men who were enemies without just cause.

On the quiet in the land they differ about who is meant. Ellicott identifies them with the pious Jews who wished to preserve their national life and religion against foreign influence. Wesley keeps it to David and his followers, who desired only to live peaceably, the enemies using not open violence but subtle artifices. Spurgeon makes the sharpest point: they love not peace, so how can they speak it — riotous men charge others with sedition.

The mockery is heard in the sound of the words. Clarke describes the cry: the last syllable of each word a protracted guttural, marking insult and triumph at once, and adds that they gaped on him in contempt. Delitzsch notices what the psalm does with that boast: the poet takes up the malignant now our eye sees it and turns it in the next verse, where the Lord is the one who has seen. Gill and Clarke press the turn — no evidence need be adduced to him who sees all.

The prayer that God should wake is handled cautiously. Gill explains that he seemed asleep to the psalmist; Clarke keeps the legal figure, that having delivered his cause into God's hand he appeals to him as judge and will abide the decision. Delitzsch parses the verbs as stirring oneself and tearing oneself from sleep, and the objects as my right, proved by facts, and my cause, to be defended. Gill then distinguishes two senses of righteousness — the imputed righteousness by which God justifies, or his essential justice in governing the world — and takes the second, judgment being asked on his cause before men, not his person before God. Clarke observes that the manner of the appeal shows the confidence David had in his innocence.

The closing wishes are read as imprecation and as prophecy. Delitzsch explains the desire to swallow him up as the climax of their wish, to clear him away so that no trace is left. Clarke translates it bluntly, we have gulped him down, and turns the whole into prediction against Saul and his courtiers, confounded and dishonoured in that last battle where Saul lost crown and life. Gill asks that they be confounded together, as one man, since together they had gathered against him. Delitzsch closes on the other side: those who wish David's righteousness made manifest take delight in it, and when it is, the Lord's own righteousness is proved — which is why David wants all who remain true to him to say, let the Lord be magnified. Gill adds who those adherents were: a few of rank, like Saul's own son, but the greatest part mean, as Christ's cause is favoured by the weak things of the world.
